  • ions across the red blood cell membrane during carbon dioxide transport. This process maintains
  • ionic balance and allows more carbon dioxide to be carried in th e blood. It is essential for proper
  • respiration and gas exchange. (Definition: 1 Mark; Mechanism: 1 mark; Significance: 1 Mark)

questions.question: Explain the role of TRH and its regulation. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of TRH and its regulation. [U]/[CO3]
  • TRH (Thyrotropin Releasing Hormone) is secreted by the hypothalamus and stimulates the
  • anterior pituitary to release TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone). TSH in turn stimulates the
  • thyroid gland to produce thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), which regulate metabolism. The secretion
  • of TRH is controlled by a negative feedback mechanism, where high levels of thyroid hormones
  • inhibit the release of TRH and TSH, while low levels stimulate their secretion. (Role of TRH: 1.5
  • marks; Regulation: 1.5 marks)

questions.question: Explain how the structure of the renal corpuscle is suited for filtration. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how the structure of the renal corpuscle is suited for filtration. [U]/[CO1]
  • The renal corpuscle is well adapted for filtration due to its specialized structure. It consists of a
  • glomerulus, a network of capillaries enclosed within Bowman’s capsule . The glomerular
  • capillaries have thin, porous walls (fenestrations) that allow easy filtration of fluids. The filtration
  • membrane (capillary wall, basement membrane and podocytes) is selectively permeable, allowing
  • small molecules to pass while preventing proteins and cells. High blood pressure in the glomerulus
  • facilitates ultrafiltration. (Structure: 1.5 marks; Function: 1.5 marks) (Liberal valuation)

questions.question: Describe mechanism of antigen- antibody reaction. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe mechanism of antigen-antibody reaction. [U]/[CO4]
  • The antigen–antibody reaction is a specific immune response in which antibodies bind to their
  • corresponding antigens to neutralize or eliminate them. Antibodies recognize antigens through
  • specific binding sites (paratopes) that fit the antigen’s epitopes like a lock and key. When binding
  • occurs, it forms an antigen–antibody complex . Agglutination: Clumping of cells or particles;
  • Precipitation: Formation of insoluble complexes from soluble antigen. Neutralization: Blocking
  • the harmful effects of toxins or pathogens. Complement activation: Leads to lysis of pathogens.
  • Opsonization: Enhances phagocytosis by marking pathogens for destruction. (Definition: 1 mark;
  • Mechanism: 1 mark; Reactions: 3 marks).

questions.question: Outline the causes and consequences of hypoxia and hypercapnia. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Outline the causes and consequences of hypoxia and hypercapnia. [U]/[CO1]
  • Hypoxia and hypercapnia are disorders of impaired gas exchange in the body. Hypoxia is mainly
  • caused by lung diseases, high altitude, anaemia, heart failure and carbon monoxide poisoning,
  • while hypercapnia results from hypoventilation due to chronic obstru ctive pulmonary disease,
  • respiratory depression from drugs, neuromuscular disorders, or airway blockage. The
  • consequences of hypoxia include fatigue, cyanosis, organ dysfunction, brain damage, and death in
  • severe cases. Hypercapnia leads to respiratory aci dosis, headaches, confusion, drowsiness and in
  • extreme situations, coma and respiratory failure. (Causes of hypoxia and hypercapnia: 2 marks;
  • Effects of hypoxia and hypercapnia: 3 marks)

questions.question: Give an account on rigor mortis. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Give an account on rigor mortis. [U]/[CO2]
  • Rigor mortis is the stiffening of muscles after death due to biochemical changes in muscle fibers.
  • After death, respiration stops and ATP production ceases. ATP is necessary for muscle relaxation,
  • so in its absence, the actin and myosin filaments remain locked, causing muscle stiffness. Rigor
  • mortis usually begins within 2 to 4 hours after death, first appearing in the small muscles of the
  • face and jaw, and then spreads to other parts of the body. It becomes fully developed in about 12
  • hours and gradually disappears after 24 to 48 hours due to muscle protein breakdown. This process
  • is important in forensic science to estimate the time of death. (Definition: 2 marks; Cause: 2 marks;
  • Importance: 1 mark)

questions.solution_html:
• Write an account on neural disorders in man. [K]/[CO2]
  • Neural disorders affect the normal functioning of the nervous system. S tructural, biochemical or
  • electrical abnormalities in the brain, spinal cord or other nerves can result in wide range of
  • symptoms. Common disorders are: Dyslexia: A learning disorder characterized by difficulty in
  • reading, writing and spelling , despite normal intelligence. Parkinson’s disease: A degenerative
  • disorder causing tremors, muscle rigidity, slow movements and poor balance . Epilepsy: A
  • neurological disorder marked by recurrent seizures, sudden loss of consciousness and uncontrolled
  • muscle movements. Alzheimer’s disease: A progressive brain disorder leading to memory loss,
  • confusion, difficulty in thinking and behavioral changes . (Definition: 1 mark; Neural Disorders
